#2458. Grading every NBA lottery pick from 2026 Draft: Yaxel Lendeborg gets an A+, plus which rookies need more time

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It's Thanksgiving. Well, almost anyway. While that's not a traditionally basketball-centric holiday, it is a useful landmark on the schedule for the NBA's crop of rookies. It's been more than a month. Teams have played about 20% of their schedules. Nobody's career trajectory is locked, but we've seen enough of everyone to start to form real opinions about who's headed where. It's fair to start to take stock of one of the more talented rookie classes in recent NBA history.

So let's grade the lottery picks from June's NBA Draft. The grades will be based primarily on the performance of the player, yes, but will also take into account where the player was picked and the circumstances that player was drafted into. Before lottery reform, the draft was designed to send the best prospects to the worst teams, after all, so not everyone was drafted into an especially desirable situation. We'll start at No. 1 and work our way down.

The raw rim numbers are iffy. The rim tape is jaw-dropping. Dybantsa is one of the most breathtaking open-court players in the NBA, an absolutely lethal downhill driver with an exceedingly rare combination of athletic tools and ball skills. Those traits alone are going to take him far.

The Wizards wasted him early in the season. They've thankfully started to shift more of the offense in his direction, but there is very little shooting on this roster and he spent most of his first dozen or so games watching Trae Young dribble. Dybantsa should never be stashed in the corner. That's true because it wastes his talents, yes, but it's also the reality of his miserable start as a jump-shooter. That's going to be the skill he needs to upgrade to reach true stardom. He doesn't need to be great at it. He just needs to be acceptable.

If he gets there, and if the Wizards can put better supporting offensive talent around him, they should be encouraged by what they've seen thus far. The ball needs to be in his hands and they're starting to embrace that. He's buying in defensively more than many rookies of his pedigree, and his combination of size and foot speed makes him a potential nightmare for opposing ball-handlers. He'll need to clean up his shooting, but otherwise, it's been a fairly strong start.

He never gets to the rim and it's becoming a bit of a problem. Rim-protectors are playing him for his floater and it's disrupting him as a driver. He'll have to get stronger to finish through contact since he simply doesn't have an elite first step. Getting Jusuf Nurkić back will be helpful in this respect. He's the least heralded of Utah's three injured bigs, but his screening is the single skill that's going to matter most to the Jazz guards. They're having so much trouble generating advantages. Nurkić will create space for them.

Peterson's finishing is a worthwhile parallel to Dybantsa's shooting. It's never going to be the selling point. It has to improve to complement his true star trait: the shooting. It has come and gone early in the season. His poor catch-and-shoot numbers aren't much of a concern. He was great in that respect at Kansas and throughout his amateur career. His pull-up shooting -- and those are the sorts of shots stars need to be able to take and make -- has been more encouraging. He's not a point guard-level passer, and the fact that Keyonte George isn't either poses long-term problems, but he's a contributor in that respect. The Jazz are still figuring that fit out, and without Jaren Jackson Jr. and Lauri Markkanen as release valves, they're both overburdened.

Give him time. Let the Jazz get healthy. He probably should have been in more of a complementary role as a rookie than he's gotten to be. That will come down the line. He recently had a five-game stretch averaging 24.4 points on almost nine 3-point attempts per game. That's his ticket to stardom: efficient, volume shooting that amplifies his floor game and playmaking.

Boozer's reputation as a winner is well-deserved. He makes a dozen little plays every night that tilt games towards the Grizzlies, and those great plays very often build off one another. He's already one of the NBA's best outlet passers, and one reason for that is how quickly his eyes dart down the floor after pulling in a rebound. It often happens while he's still in the air. He's better defensively than most rookies at this point because he just doesn't make the basic mistakes rookies -- especially rookie bigs -- so often make. He's almost always in the right place at the right time. He leads the rookie class in plus-minus pretty comfortably at +74. Don't make a habit of using that as a measure of individual performance, but it underlines the simple reality that good things happen when Boozer is on the floor.

So why the minus? Boozer's scoring is still pretty inefficient. The 3-point shooting will come around. He just had a 7 of 13 game against the Wizards that showed what he can be from deep. That he's below 49% on 2s is a bit more concerning. Boozer basically never shoots mid-range jumpers, and things that worked in college aren't working in quite the same way in the NBA. He can't bully NBA-level defenders as easily as he could their college counterparts. He's not especially vertical either, so he's been blocked from behind a few times.

He's going to need a go-to move or two near the basket, and he's probably going to have to develop his floater into a more consistent tool. The latter will only further weaponize his passing, especially with Zach Edey near the rim and so much shooting around him. We're not talking about a post-up exclusive player here either. Boozer is so comfortable as a driver for his size that he'll have plenty of options, and if the 3-point shot does come along, it will only make this sort of growth easier.

The Bulls are really letting Wilson explore the studio space. The mistakes are loud. The highlights are louder. He can absolutely fly, and wearing this uniform, that says something. Wilson practically never lays the ball up. If he's near the basket, he's dunking. What's most notable here is what's happening when he's not near the basket. Wilson took just 27 3s at North Carolina. He's taking more than seven per game for the Bulls, more than any rookie but Darius Acuff. Chicago, under a different regime, nudged Matas Buzelis in this direction last year as well. The Bulls want their athletic wings to be 3-point shooters and they're willing to accept clunky offense to get there.

Wilson is going to be a monster defensive playmaker. His length, athleticism and aggression already jump out of the screen, and he easily leads all rookies in steals and deflections per game. His work on the ball and in pick-and-roll is going to be a work in progress, and he has to get stronger. The Bulls don't have a true rim-protector on the roster yet, so judging just about anyone is tricky.

The Bulls were the worst team in the NBA when Wilson was playing and are 4-3 since he got hurt. Buzelis in particular has hit his stride without having to devote so much of the offense to developing the franchise player, and that's worth monitoring as the Bulls are betting big on their partnership moving forward. Still, this is probably the right approach for a Bulls team going nowhere in the next few years. Let Wilson play through his mistakes, tighten up his handle and try to build a decent jumper. There is a star in here somewhere and we're already seeing signs of it in his rookie season.

Wagler is the obvious post-deadline rookie breakout candidate to watch. Ty Lue has never loved playing young players, and sure enough, Wagler's playing time has been inconsistent early on. When the Clippers inevitably trade a bunch of veterans in February, we'll get more of him. Hopefully by then he'll have found ways to compensate for how ridiculously slow he is. Scoring inside of the arc has been an adventure for Wagler because he just can't get by anyone. If the NBA tracked the rate of drives in which a defender moves in total lockstep with the ball-handler for so long that said ball-handler just sort of throws up a contested prayer, Wagler would be near the top of the league.

Getting to the rim, fortunately, is not his bread and butter. Wagler is already a stellar foul-drawer. He has nearly 50% more made free throws than field goal attempts. He's putting up a ton of 3s as well and making a reasonable chunk of them. He's not exactly Tyrese Haliburton on the break, but the Clippers are a far, far better transition offense with him on the floor. He's going to need more reps to learn how to play around his flaws, but this shot profile with a low-turnover point guard is a very promising prospect.

Brown has had the toughest go of it so far among the four point guards picked in a row. The emergence of Nolan Traoré has mostly kept him out of the starting lineup, and Brooklyn's odd decision to trade for Julius Randle has left the Nets with more mouths to feed than a team this bad should really have. That has made it hard for Brown to find much of a rhythm as a rookie. When the jump shots fall, he's valuable. When they don't, he hasn't been able to impact games consistently, and his rim finishing has been a mess. He often feels rushed as a driver, but that's common for rookie guards.

Brown got his first start in Brooklyn's last game, a loss to the Minnesota Timberwolves, and it was his best game as a professional. His reads in pick-and-roll were impressive and he's starting to get a better grasp on where help is coming from and how he can punish it with his passing. With Traoré now hurt, Brown figures to be a starter moving forward, and hopefully that gets his rookie year on track.

Most of the concerns about Acuff's playing style are overblown. He is not some empty-calorie chucker. Acuff's efficiency is in line with most of the other top picks, and he's doing it on substantially higher volume. He has a nearly 2-to-1 assist-to-turnover ratio. Sacramento's offense dies whenever he sits. His All Star-level counting stats don't make him an All-Star, but he's generating better team offense than anyone else on this miserable roster and most of this rookie class for that matter. To get these numbers out of a No. 7 overall pick, regardless of context, represents an almost absolute victory.

That doesn't mean Sacramento is managing him flawlessly. There should be some real fear here that the Kings are teaching Acuff lessons he won't be able to unlearn. He's taking more shots per game than Jalen Brunson, Tyrese Maxey, Dwyane Wade or Derrick Rose ever did. Is he going to be able to scale down when his roster eventually calls for it? The danger in letting a rookie ball-handler have this long a leash is that it gives them an excuse not to develop the off-ball skills that good teams actually need even out of their primary ball-handlers. Think Trae Young. His defense is, predictably, a disaster. The shooting is almost all off the dribble. He's not the most eager cutter.

The bar for stardom out of this player type is enormously high. He's going to have to become, say, a Damian Lillard-esque shooter to cover up his existing flaws if he doesn't improve them with time. That's possible, but it's not likely for basically anyone. Letting Acuff grow like this as a scorer is, generally, wise. He's the only true building block this team has. Maybe tone it down 10% and try to round him out a bit, if not now, then in the near future when you've had time to change the roster around him.

Boozer got the "winner" rep in this draft class, but Flemings is the closest thing this guard class has to one. His motor is infectious on both ends of the floor, particularly on defense, and his aggression as a driver will only get more powerful as he's surrounded by better shooters. He doesn't take many 3s, but he's making the ones he's taking and holding up well in mid-range. There's a path to "pretty good" when it comes to his shooting, which is all he'll need given his speed and playmaking.

We're still dealing with relatively small samples here, but his on-off numbers with Jalen Johnson are worth monitoring. The Hawks are great when either plays without the other and terrible when they're on the floor together. Flemings' numbers, in particular, bolt upward when he gets to play without Atlanta's resident All-Star, and that makes sense when you think about how rim-dependent Johnson is. The floor is more open for Flemings when he plays without him, but these are two of the most important players on the roster moving forward. They have to figure out how to coexist, especially now that Flemings is starting for the injured CJ McCollum.

Fair or not, Dusty May is forever going to be attached to this pick. How influential he was in selecting Johnson, we may never know, but for what it's worth, that pick had Masai Ujiri written all over it. So does this roster, which is stuffed to the gills with the sort of rangy, athletic forwards that always populated Ujiri's Raptors teams. Johnson is redundant here. He's playing center full-time when his best defensive position is probably power forward. He's not offering much offensively besides his rebounding. He's going to be a real NBA player; he's just exactly the sort of player a team with Cooper Flagg, Naji Marshall, PJ Washington and Zaccharie Risacher didn't need.

Again... we don't know how much influence May had on the pick. But the Mavericks had a massive information advantage over the field when it came to his three lottery-bound Michigan Wolverines. They had their pick out of the trio. One of them is a star, the other is off to a great start, and both offer skill sets this team needed more of. Dallas is dying for more shooting. We have no idea when or if Dereck Lively will get healthy, so adding a true long-term center should be a priority. Johnson may yet be the best Michigan player in this class down the line. For now, he's just not in a position to succeed, and he looks like the worst of Michigan's three lottery picks.

It took Burries a month to start hitting 3s, but now that he is, the theory of him as a player is starting to come together. He's not just a 3-and-D player, but 3-and-D are going to be centerpiece skills for him. He's probably never going to be a primary scorer, but he's going to affect games in a lot of other ways.

He's already one of the NBA's best rebounding guards, for example. He's further along as a ball-handler than expected as well, already able to kill closeouts and make real reads in pick-and-roll. He's on the wrong team for this sort of skill set. He's meant to amplify great players, not shoulder a heavy burden on a team with minimal shot-creation. That's a Bucks problem. Burries is doing his part thus far, and if the 3s keep going in, he's headed for a very nice rookie year.

I thought about an "S." As in S-tier. Or savior. He's struggled since Stephen Curry went down. Fine. There's no other shot-creation on this roster. He turns the ball over. That's closer to a feature than a bug given the motion system Golden State uses. You'd rather not have players chirping at Luka Dončić. Negatives addressed.

Yaxel Lendeborg is headed for stardom. We were told he was going to be a 3-and-D player in the NBA. He's self-creating 3s like a seasoned star. He's filling in for the absent Jimmy Butler in a number of unforeseeable ways. He's one of the only players on this team that gets to the line. He's a real playmaker, averaging more assists per game out of drives than Giannis Antetokounmpo. His on-ball defense is as advertised. When Steve Kerr publicly called out his off-ball defense, he took it and improved. If there were maturity concerns here, they certainly haven't affected his coachability thus far.

The degree to which Lendeborg altered Golden State's trajectory can't be understated. The Warriors looked primed for a stealth tank before the season began. They didn't want to lose, per se, but they did little to actually, actively improve around a 38-year-old Curry and seemed pleased with the idea of three lottery balls in May. Now they have a foundational player on a rookie deal for four years, and if Butler returns at anything close to full strength, they'll be close enough to posing a meaningful threat in the playoffs to potentially justify trading a pick or two for help (ideally in the form of a shooting center, but perhaps another scorer as well). They're not going to win the championship, but they're a real team again because they picked one of the two best rookies in this class outside of the top 10. If nothing else, Curry's career gets to end with some dignity because Lendeborg will be on his team.

The Thunder are missing defenders everywhere. They still give up basically nothing at the basket when Mara is on the floor. He's much more mobile than a center of his size has any right to be. He's fourth in the NBA in total dunks despite playing only about 22 minutes per night. His passing is going to become a real value-add over time, especially on a Thunder team that tends to move the ball minimally for the sake of avoiding turnovers. His reflexes are lightning quick in this respect. If a defender is napping off-ball for even a second, Mara will hit someone for a back cut.

Is there star-level upside here? Probably not, and the defensive rebounding probably needs to be a bit better. Still, think of the price that teams are paying even for non-star centers lately. Walker Kessler and Ivica Zubac each netted premium draft returns. That made Mara's draft night slide so surprising. As the NBA pivots back towards size after years of pace-and-space, demand is severely outpacing supply at center. For the Thunder to get someone with a chance to be as valuable as Kessler or Zubac outside of the top 10 is yet another draft night home run for Sam Presti.

His role has been fairly limited thus far, but he's doing what he can in the position that he's in. Offensively, it's basically all catch-and-shoot and transition. That's fine. The Bucks can slowly layer in on-ball opportunities. It's the combination of size and shooting that's so tantalizing here, and Ament is shooting very well on his open looks. He has a ways to go everywhere else, but the Bucks frankly have the time to develop him at his own pace.

He's taken the challenge of defending tough assignments reasonably well by rookie standards. He's no stopper, but he's played hard and held his own. His off-ball defense needs work. That's typically a skill that comes a bit later, and not all players who get excited about guarding opposing stars are as diligent about that aspect of defense. He got his second start against Portland last Thursday and delivered his best game as a professional. The Bucks need to get Kyle Kuzma out of here so they can give Ament the full-time starting slot he'll need to grow.

He's barely played. The skill that got him drafted in the lottery -- rebounding -- has mostly shown up in the scant minutes he's received. There's just not much we can learn out of 68 total minutes. The Hornets just have a very deep frontcourt and few shot-creating guards with which to support those forwards and centers. Allen Graves and Bennett Stirtz have made real impacts from this range of the draft, but remember, the Hornets also picked at No. 17 and got Christian Anderson, who's impressed early in his rookie season as well. We can't exactly write Steinbach off. We just haven't seen enough of him to say much definitively yet.

#2457. NFL Week 12 picks: Our experts face off on Broncos at Steelers, Seahawks at 49ers and more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Welcome to the most special week in the NFL. We watched the Los Angeles Rams defeat the Green Bay Packers on Wednesday night, and now, we have three exciting Thanksgiving matchups to digest this "Turkey Day."

Football fans suffered through many sleepy Chicago Bears vs. Detroit Lions Thanksgiving matchups over the years. Now, this 1 p.m. game on Thursday is expected to be one of the most exciting holiday matchups in recent memory. After that, the Dallas Cowboys will welcome Joe Milton III and the Philadelphia Eagles to AT&T Stadium. Both teams are coming off wins, and the Cowboys need this game if they want to keep pace in the NFC East. At the end of the night, we have a potential AFC Championship preview to watch when the Buffalo Bills host Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs. This is just the second game in NFL history to feature two teams coming off at least three straight 17-point victories.

Which teams should you pick in Week 12, and which should you fade? CBS Sports writers Jordan Dajani and Jared Dubin are here to break down the biggest games of the weekend. For clarity, lines for these selections were taken on Nov. 25 over at DraftKings Sportsbook.

Dajani (Broncos -3.5): Aaron Rodgers lobbed a grenade into the Pittsburgh Steelers facility as he exited it this week. Going on national television and calling your coach a narcoleptic, unhealthy, lazy person who doesn't even know the franchise he works for is insane. So, this is a moment that will ultimately rally the locker room, or cause them to completely fall apart. Pick which side you'd like. The Steelers have also won and covered in six straight home games. This seems like an appropriate time for that streak to end   …  Prediction: Broncos 20, Steelers 13

Dubin (Broncos -3.5): After the disaster that hit the Steelers this week, I just can't see them keeping the game close against the Broncos. No, I don't think they'll get the backup quarterback bounce from Mason Rudolph. I don't trust the Broncos as far as Bo Nix or I can throw them, but given the state the Steelers' locker room has to be in right now, I think you have to roll with Denver to cover this one with relative ease.  … Prediction: Broncos 24, Steelers 10

Dajani (Ravens +7): I have the Houston Texans winning this game, but seven points seems a bit high. C.J. Stroud is playing some great football, but his production has been overshadowed by a defense that has fallen from No. 2 in points allowed per game in 2025, to 17th this year. The Texans are 1-8 against the spread in their last nine home games following an ATS win. I'll take Baltimore to keep it close… Prediction: Texans 24, Ravens 18

Dubin (Ravens +7): The Ravens have now lost six straight, but they've lost the two games in the Jacoby Brissett era by a combined five points despite turning the ball over six times in those contests. If they can just limit the giveaways, I think they might even be able to pull off an upset against a Houston team that hasn't exactly lit the world on fire this year. Either way, I think they can keep it close by throwing on a surprisingly vulnerable Texans pass defense.  … Prediction: Texans 24, Ravens 20

Dajani (49ers -3): Sam Darnold is expected to return this week, and he's accounted for 10 touchdowns compared to nine interceptions in seven starts this season. If you throw out the season opener that Drew Lock finished and won, Darnold is 2-4 as a starter this season.

Believe it or not, San Francisco is 0-9 against the spread in its last nine home divisional games. With the number at a field goal, the 49ers have a good chance to end that streak this week. What they did to the Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City last Sunday night was shocking. The 49ers should be headlining everyone's NFL power rankings if they weren't already. Their 0.19 EPA per play is the best mark since the 2018 Chiefs, and they have the best offensive success rate (54.8%) by any team in a season since at least 2000 …  Prediction: 49ers 24, Seahawks 20

Dubin (49ers -3): I reserve the right to flip this prediction to Seattle if Brock Purdy is out with his ankle injury, but if he's in, I just think that this San Francisco offense is a buzzsaw that can't really be stopped — even by the Dark Side defense. Remember, they dropped 32 points on Seattle the last time out. And they've scored 35 or more in each of their three games since returning from the bye. I don't think they can be stopped when everyone is healthy.  … Prediction: 49ers 30, Seahawks 23

Dajani (Raiders +4.5): Maybe part of me is rooting for Fernando Mendoza in his first primetime start? Last week against the Broncos, he threw for 267 yards, three touchdowns and an interception. It was a solid performance, even though the rookie was sacked five times. The Raiders certainly have their weaknesses. They are on pace to become the first team since the 2022 Texans to finish bottom two in both rushing yards per game and opponent rushing yards per game, but this 6-4 Cleveland Browns team hasn't won a game by five-plus points since LAST YEAR. That gives me some optimism Vegas can cover  …  Prediction: Browns 24, Raiders 20

Dubin (Raiders +4.5): I will continue to stand on the idea that this Browns team is not good. Every one of Cleveland's wins has required a game-winning drive in the final minutes of the fourth quarter. The Browns have been out-gained in seven of their 10 games and are somehow 6-4. That is not remotely sustainable. I think the Raiders pull off the upset behind Fernando Mendoza and a returning Brock Bowers. … Prediction: Raiders 21, Browns 17

Dajani (Panthers +3): I'm going to take the points with the Panthers because they are playing on the road. If you were unaware, Carolina is 3-2 away from Charlotte, and has a +8 turnover differential. The Panthers have a -4 turnover differential at home, and allow 37.4 points per game at Bank of America Stadium! For whatever reason, the Panthers are a better team on the road.

It's true that the Tampa Bay Buccaneers throttled the Panthers in Week 7, 43-13, but I think Carolina splits the season series. The Buccaneers are 1-9 against the spread in their last 10 home games, and 0-7 against the spread in their last seven home primetime games. Baker Mayfield is a shocking 1-13 in primetime since 2021, so I'll back Bryce Young …  Prediction: Panthers 28, Buccaneers 27

Dubin (Buccaneers -3): The last time these two teams played, the Bucs racked up 258 rushing yards. The Panthers' run defense then limited the Packers, Broncos and Saints over the next three games, but the Ravens hit them up for 157 yards last week. I don't see much reason to believe that the Bucs will be slowed on the ground, and I don't trust Carolina's offense to score enough to get the Bucs out of their run-heavy orientation.  … Prediction: Buccaneers 20, Panthers 16

Dajani (Bears -1.5): I can't remember being more excited for a Thanksgiving Day game, as the Bears and Lions are two of the best teams in the NFL. What I keep going back to is that the Bears are 6-0 while averaging 33.7 points in games where Caleb Williams starts and finishes. Then, factor in how much improved this Chicago defense looks with the addition of Jeffery Simmons. In Weeks 1-7, they ranked dead last in both yards per play (6.3) and yards per attempt (8.7). Over the last four weeks, the Bears now rank in the top 10 in both categories. Chicago has been swept by Detroit in each of the last two seasons. I think the Bears are done with losing to Dan Campbell …  Prediction: Bears 30, Lions 28

Dubin (Lions +1.5): These are two incredibly evenly-matched teams, but it seems like Detroit has more matchup advantages offensively against Chicago's improved defense than the Bears do against the Lions' own improved unit. With Detroit also getting the benefit of home-field advantage, we're rolling with the Lions to win a close one as a home underdog.  … Prediction: Lions 31, Bears 30

Dajani (Cowboys -8.5): I don't think the Cowboys have exorcised all of their defensive demons just because they blew out the Tennessee Titans, but that win at home was just what this team needed. This is one of those cases where I think the Cowboys just simply out-score their opponent. This is still a rivalry, but the Eagles are 2-8 against the spread this season, which ranks second-worst in the NFL behind the Los Angeles Chargers, and are 0-5 against the spread in their last five divisional matchups. The Cowboys should get this cover in the fourth quarter. They have scored NINETY-ONE (91) points over the past two games! That's the most in a two-game span since 1971…  Prediction: Cowboys 33, Eagles 20

Dubin (Eagles +8.5): I know they just beat the Titans by 21, but I don't like laying this many points with the Cowboys. Their defense is still too suspect and they are still too prone to games where they don't perform up to expectations for me to be comfortable with an 8.5-point spread. So even while I think they'll dent the scoreboard at home on Thanksgiving afternoon, I can't bring myself to predict that this will be a blowout. … Prediction: Cowboys 30, Eagles 24

Dajani (Chiefs +3): The craziest part about this rivalry is that the Bills have won the last five regular-season meetings, while the Chiefs have won the last four playoff meetings! You should also know that the weather is supposed to be terrible on Thursday night, so this could come down to which team runs the ball better. James Cook has recorded nine straight games with 75 rushing yards and a touchdown. He and Josh Allen are the second duo to ever account for double-digit rushing touchdowns each through the first 10 games of a season. Meanwhile, on the other side, Emmett Johnson has rushed for 206 yards with 108 receiving yards and three touchdowns over the last two games in place of the injured Kenneth Walker III. I almost think a three-point spread in this matchup is pretty high. That's going to lead me to take the points even though Bills over Chiefs has been an auto-bet in the regular season recently… Prediction: Chiefs 17, Bills 16

Dubin (Bills -3): I have basically the exact same analysis of this game as Dajani but come down on the opposite side of the bet because of the Bills' regular-season history against the Chiefs and the relative strength of their run game. I trust Josh Allen and James Cook to run the ball more than I do Emmett Johnson, even with how good Johnson has been over the last two weeks. Could Patrick Mahomes make this prediction look silly? Of course. But I think that'll prove more difficult in Thursday night's expected weather. … Prediction: Bills 21, Chiefs 17

#2456. Even Pellerud, a titan of women’s coaching, talks winning the Euros and World Cup

Even Pellerud is one of a select amount of head coaches who can say he won both a European Championship and a World Cup. He can also say he coached in a further two European finals and won an Olympic bronze medal. Not bad.

The 68-year-old is one of the most decorated coaches in the history of the women’s game at international level, with all his success coming with his home nation of Norway, while he also had a nine-year spell as Canada head coach where he pushed forward the development of the women’s game across the pond.

Across an hour-long interview from his home back in Norway, Pellerud reflects on what he constantly describes as a “lucky” career – not necessarily in terms of he didn’t work hard, but that he is privileged to have enjoyed so much success, especially when he discusses just how little he knew of the women’s game when he was asked by the Norwegian Football Federation to lead the women’s national team in the late 1980s.

After retiring from playing in 1986 and taking over as manager for the team he’d last played for, it was in 1989 that Pellerud’s coaching career took a new path, a path he would not look back from. “It was a strange incident really,” he chuckles. “I was asked to meet the federation. My name had started to grow a little bit, but I was kind of expecting it to be maybe one of the men’s youth teams.

“In the meeting, they offered me the job of the women’s team and that was a big shock for me. I think I had the right attitude for it, but I hadn’t actually seen one women’s game in my life, not even on TV.”

He adds, “They seemed to think I was the man for the job. I was ready to move on, so I was motivated and I wanted to be part of that environment, to grow something, that’s what really triggered me to do it. All I asked is that I have a contract for only two years, because I didn’t know how it would go.”

Two years would become seven, and an unprecedented period of success for Norway which saw Pellerud lead his nation to a European Championship in 1993, and after coming up short in the final of the inaugural World Cup in 1991, the grandest prize of all two years later in 1995, plus an Olympic bronze one year later in 1996, Pellerud’s final tournament of his first spell with Norway.

“To cut a long story short, I fell in love with the team,” he smiles. “We had a very strong team, a lot of success, I had a lot of fun. It was a great team to coach, such characters, such committed players. They were fit, well trained, it was just a fun team to work with and there was a lot of work to do, but it was a great job. It ended up being seven fantastic years.”

Pellerud inherited a side that included players who would go down in legend. Captain Heidi Støre, future Team GB head coach Hege Riise, one of Europe’s finest goalkeepers Bente Nordby and hotshot striker Linda Medalen, among many others.

Norway had won the first unofficial World Cup in 1988, but with a lack of footage, analysis or any of the things a modern-day coach would now have access to, a novice in the women’s game had no real understanding of where his squad of players was at heading into the World Cup, so how did he do it?

“That is a good question,” he exclaims. “Norwegian players in the league played in front of 50 spectators, in small venues, no media, they were playing games we won quite easily with the national team. It was only when we met Germany, Sweden or Denmark we were challenged.”

Pellerud, therefore, took his side to Winnipeg in Canada for a tournament against said hosts and the USA in 1990 to get a better understanding of what challenges he would face come the first World Cup in China, which was just a year down the line.

“That was the biggest eye-opener for me,” he recalls. “I was so happy we had that challenge. We beat Canada, but the USA just played us off the field, we had no chance. I think we lost 4-0 and it was a real shocker for me. I knew they were good because in 1988 the USA were the best team, even though Norway won, the coaches told me the USA were the best team. It was an eye-opener as to what to expect in China. We flew home and had some serious chats about what to do, how to bridge that gap in the space of a year.”

Pellerud admits going into the opening game, against the hosts, he had no real idea of what to expect, it was a whole other world to what his players had experienced back home, with the locals absorbing and engaging with the tournament on a level the women’s game hadn’t seen before.

“We went from these small games in Norway to 65,000 fans in China. Stands filled with people, we’d been in Europe and not seen this. My eyes were opened. Big buses, police escorts, people in the streets, it was so big you can lose yourself a bit. You don’t feel connected to the games or your team. The sound, the music, the opening ceremony, I will never forget the hours in the changing room after the opening game.”

Norway had lost 4-0 to hosts China and looked a world away from a side that would reach the final just a few weeks later. Pellerud and his side had been completely taken aback by what lay in front of them and had to act quick to ensure their tournament got back on track.

“We started well, we missed a penalty, but after that we didn’t have the ball, China totally outplayed us. That was my first World Cup game, you can imagine. We had to learn quickly how to raise a team that wasn’t used to losing, and here we are losing 4-0. They were rough days and for me, I learned a lot in that period.”

They bounced back to beat New Zealand 4-0 and Denmark 2-1, progressing past Italy in a dramatic and enthralling quarter-final, before disposing of neighbours Sweden in style with a 4-1 semi-final win.

The final didn’t go their way, a last-gasp Michelle Akers goal sealing the tournament for the USA, but Pellerud and his side had come so far from their 4-0 loss to the same opposition a year earlier, and had set the foundations for what was to come.

“We knew we had that level. We knew we had the players and we had the support from the federation,” he says. “The main thing for us was to create an environment where the players could be challenged enough in the league games. That was issue number one. We had to compensate for that by being super fit, super organised, we worked so much on defending. We had to introduce girls to training with the boys just to step them up a little bit. We had some really good years.”

“Good” is perhaps an understatement. Pellerud became European champion in 1993 when Birthe Hegstad’s late goal sealed a win in the final against Italy, before they headed to neighbouring Sweden in 1995 with renewed vigour ahead of the second World Cup. Riise was named player of the tournament and striker Ann Kristin Aarønes was the top scorer in the tournament with six goals, with Riise just behind on five. No other player for any country scored more than three.

Norway dominated from day one, winning all three group games without conceding and scoring an incredible 17 goals. They beat Nigeria 8-0, England 2-0 and Canada 7-0. A 3-1 win against Denmark in the quarter-finals was followed by the toughest test of all and a 1-0 win against defending champions USA.

Germany stood in their way of glory, but goals from Riise and Marianne Pettersen ensured it was Pellerud who came away as a world champion, and he admits he knew throughout the tournament his team would come out on top, and the feeling of being a world champion has only grown stronger in the subsequent 27 years.

“At the time, you live by the day, live by the training, live by the next game,” he says. “You don’t think so much about it, but I have to say in the years since it gets bigger and bigger for me. It was one of the tournaments where everything flies in your direction, everything we did was a success.

“We lost our captain in the semi-final against USA. Usually, we should be concerned, but we weren’t, we knew we were going to win. That is a very rare feeling for a coach. I’ve had that maybe twice in my life, that nobody was going to beat us.”

On the final itself, he recalls, “We pressed Germany super high. They got frustrated, we had full control, both games against them and USA was an extreme example of competitiveness, but not beauty. None of these games were beautiful. They were tough, a struggle, just don’t make mistakes, take your chances. But for the neutral, it was not fancy football. If Hege Riise and Linda Medalen and others played today, they would have been stars. The talent, the understanding of the game, the brilliant football minds. With today’s facilities, they would be stars.”

After a bronze medal one year later at the Atlanta Olympics which saw hosts USA win out in another tight semi-final, Pellerud stepped away and returned to the men’s game, but his affiliation with the women’s game was far from over. “The Olympics was another huge highlight in my life, but we weren’t quite as good, not quite as sharp, that was my feeling and I was right. I had many offers to coach men’s teams and had a desire in me to do that again.

“I’d got divorced and moved away from my home town, there were different things in my life which were both exciting and difficult. I was actually offered a lifetime contract with the federation.”

After a spell with Norwegian side Lillestrøm, Pellerud became the first Norwegian to coach a top division side in Denmark when he took over at Ikast FC. Three years since his last involvement in the women’s game, the opportunity soon arose to go back into it with another exciting new challenge.

“The General Secretary in Canada called me to discuss a contract to coach the women’s team. They had been very unsuccessful in 1991, 1995 and 1999 and wanted a European coach. It was a good fit in many ways. I’d remarried, we had two young twin daughters and we agreed on a mutual desire to see something of the world before the girls became too old. We went to Toronto, met the people, got a house, and like in Norway, two years became nine years!”

While now an experienced coach in the women’s game, Pellerud’s challenge almost outweighed that of him walking into the women’s game a decade previous with no knowledge of the sport, such was Canada’s position at the time.

After failing to qualify for the first World Cup, Canada went out at the group stage in both 1995 and 1999 and there was a lot of work to do for a country that was yet to embrace the sport of soccer.

“It’s almost impossible to think about,” says Pellerud of the challenge of taking on the Canada job. “It was not a soccer country then, there was no soccer on the news, no writing about it. The only information I had was that all my players after the 1999 World Cup were released from their contract. They said it was up to me if I wanted to bring anyone back.

“I didn’t complicate things, I ran around the country to see games that were set up as trials for the national team so I could see the best players in each province. I started to pick a team, had a camp in British Columbia and I used my contacts back in Europe to get us into the Algarve Cup in 2000.

Canada held their own with what was largely a brand-new side filled with young players, losing 4-0 to China, only 2-1 to Pellerud’s former employers and ending with a 2-1 win against Finland, followed by a 3-2 win against Denmark in the fifth-place match, a certain fresh-faced teenager by the name of Christine Sinclair scoring twice.

“Everything happened so fast, so fast. I had to take risks and I got a lot right, but some wrong. I had a couple of good leaders, then I had Christine Sinclair, that was the biggest thing. When I saw her in one of the setup games, I was quick to decide she would come to the Algarve with us. She was 16, but she was very special, so I built the team around these few players and played a very simple game. We pushed things, these players went from training twice a week to twice a day.

“We did ok, the federation was very helpful. We went to tournaments, we lost a lot, then we lost a little bit less, then we started to tie games and then we started to win. I promised the team we would beat the USA within a year, that was a bold statement, but we did. We beat them in the fall of 2000 in the USA, that was a very big moment for everyone.”

By the time the 2003 World Cup came around, Pellerud had been working on developing the Canada team for almost four years, but they still very much crossed the border to their tournament hosts as underdogs compared to the bigger nations. Pellerud though had a bit of “lucky timing” as he puts it, as FIFA introduced the first Under-20 World Cup a year earlier in 2002, to be held in Canada.

Given how young his senior squad was, many of them qualified for the tournament and indeed took part under the guidance of his assistant head coach, Ian Bridge. The squad would include six players who had gone to the senior World Cup a year later – Sasha Andrews, Carmelina Moscato, Brittany Timko, Kara Lang, Erin McLeod and Sinclair.

Canada reached the final, topping their group, before Sinclair scored an incredible five goals in a 6-1 win over England, another in a penalty shootout win against Brazil, before a narrow 1-0 loss to the USA in the final, but a core of Pellerud’s youngsters had gained valuable tournament experience.

“We had that advantage because these players came through together, they knew each other so well, had already played for the senior team and some got very good scholarships to go to the USA. That 2002 group was so talented, many went to 2003 and many others went to future tournaments. Some went on to play for Canada for years and years, so it was lucky for us with the timing.”

A year later, Pellerud led Canada out of a World Cup group for the first time and their dream journey continued with a 1-0 win against China in the quarter-finals. A 2-1 loss after two goals from Sweden in the final ten minutes denied Canada what would have been an incredible appearance in the World Cup final, but Pellerud had led them further than anyone could have imagined.

It meant expectations were high four years later when Pellerud took his team to his fourth World Cup, back in China where his journey had started 16 years earlier. The likes of Sinclair were now leaders of the team, while they’d been joined by other 2002 squad members such as Melanie Booth, Robyn Gayle, Andrea Neil, Tanya Dennis, Diana Matheson, Candace Chapman, Amy Walsh, Katie Thorlakson and Taryn Swiatek.

After defeat to Norway in their opening game, qualification was between them and final group opponents Australia. When Sinclair scored with five minutes to go it looked like Canada had narrowly avoided elimination, only for Cheryl Salisbury’s 92nd-minute goal to send Pellerud and his side home early.

“Oh yes … Australia,” he reflects. “We overachieved in 2003, we had some really good players, but at the same time we had major issues with funding moving forward. The federation didn’t care much, we basically lost all our funding, so we weren’t able to maintain that level. We trained a lot, maybe we trained too hard, maybe I asked too much of them. We had injuries so didn’t go to 2007 full strength or where we should be. It was disappointing.”

Pellerud went to another Olympics oneayear later but, after another narrow defeat to the USA, this time in extra-time, Pellerud decided that not only was it time to step away, but retire from coaching altogether. “It was always one goal. We could be competitive but we didn’t have the level to control games. We had to rely on Sinclair. The timing for a new coach was great because at this time these players were reaching their peaks. It was a solid foundation, so it was the right time for a new coach to come in with a new view.”

Pellerud had a deal in place to move into the shadows in a development role with MLS side Vancouver Whitecaps, but no less than a month after leaving the Canada role, another national team offer within the women’s game arrived in his inbox. It was from Trinidad and Tobago, very much still a developing nation in the women’s game and an even bigger challenge than Canada.

“I had a deal in Vancouver, then this thing with Trindad and Tobago came up and I was very surprised by it,” he recalls. “I didn’t know much about them, but it was a development opportunity to work with young players and that’s what I wanted.

“It was a fun experience. Different, not always easy, it was the opposite of easy, but I had good local staff. The general mentality was not really team orientated. There were social problems, getting a commitment was not easy and for me to try and get the best out of them was hard. We tightened discipline, we trained a lot and trained hard, but we started to increase the number of players and started to have a team that looked like a soccer team.”

After four years helping to develop the sport in the Caribbean, Pellerud was offered the chance to go back to where it all began – back to the Norway national team ahead of the 2013 Euros and the 2015 World Cup.

Norway was about to welcome an exciting group of bright young players including Ada Hegerberg, Caroline Graham Hansen, Maren Mjelde and Ingrid Engen. “There were some rumours Norway was looking for a technical director. I showed interest but they changed their mind, so that job no longer existed. Then someone said they were going to change their coach and would I be interested? I said ‘hell yes’, so I went for a meeting and the job was mine.”

It had been 17 years since Pellerud had last coached the national team and was welcomed by a completely new squad of players, but some of the brightest young players anywhere in Europe. “A lot had changed, but also a lot hadn’t changed,” he says. “Sometimes it felt like the world had stood still. I had the same number of support staff, even with Canada I had more. In 2013, nothing was really that different to 1995, that was surprising for me.

“I think perhaps they had rested too much on successes from the 1990s and not moved forward. I really liked the players though, it was a really talented group.”

With 18-year-old duo Hegerberg and Graham Hansen gaining plenty of attention and experienced heads such as Ingrid Hjelmseth, Solveig Gulbrandsen and captain Ingvild Stensland, expectations were high for the Euros in 2013.

Pellerud once again reached a major final, losing only 1-0, while missing two penalties, in a tightly contested final with Germany, but Pellerud was more circumspect in a different stage of his career and despite the defeat, talks of his return to Norway as one of the fondest times of his career.

“I had a fantastic time,” he smiles. “If you jump to the team I came back to, I was shocked by what I saw. The skill, the ball control, the agility, the love of the game and the intense play. That was another level, and there were many of them, not just the big names.

“I could not believe what Caroline could do with a ball, to me it was just unreal. What is going on here?! I had been so many years away and not really seen her. She was 17 when I came in, but what she did for me between 2013 and 2015 was unreal. She wasn’t a mature player then, but had pure talent, speed, agility, the solutions in tight situations. She was the closest I’d seen to the best men’s players.”

Pellerud’s last hurrah would come two years later at the 2015 World Cup, ironically held in Canada, and if not for a second-round defeat against England, his last game as a national team head coach could have come between the two nations he spent most of his coaching career with.

While Hegerberg’s emergence as one of the best young strikers in the world had plenty of eyes on Norway, Pellerud lost Hansen to injury before the tournament and despite a respectable draw against Germany in the groups, Norway bowed out after losing 2-1 to England despite taking a 1-0 lead.

“I was so happy and motivated going into 2015. The team was good, but I had some concerns because we had major problems with injuries, a lot of injuries. Caroline was not there at all, but we still did ok, we should have beaten England.”

He admits he had no idea going into the tournament that it would be his last, his departure was not pre-planned, but he quickly decided after that defeat that now past the age of 60, it was time to walk away. “After that game, I knew,” he reflects. “That was it for me. I went straight to the technical director. I said ‘you don’t even have to try and ask’, but he said take a holiday and call me again in 14 days. I said ‘you can call me, but it doesn’t matter’. He did call me and I said I didn’t have the motivation or the energy to raise a team again. It was actually a very easy decision for me and I went into a new position within the federation.”

Pellerud got the technical director role he’d applied for in the first place, a role he kept until 2018, and admits his days as a head coach are done, but he’s not against helping others via his own experiences.

More importantly, though, he ends our interview reflecting back on that “lucky” feeling, appreciating every day what he achieved across a 26-year career at international level, and the medals and memories he still cherishes. “I really wake up every morning and appreciate something I just regard as being there at the right time, I was the lucky one,” he says. “I’m healthy, I met amazing people, met amazing friends. I used to compete against them, but now I see them in hotels, airplanes, I was just so lucky.

“I cherish those years very much and it makes me happy now to be able to mentor young coaches. I enjoy travelling and meeting them and being an instructor on the UEFA Pro Licence courses. It helps me meet the next generation of coaches and to help them…with no ambition of taking their jobs.”

#2455. Sons of LeBron James, Carmelo Anthony among notable college basketball players with family ties to NBA

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the best parts about Thanksgiving is reuniting with family, eating good food and watching sports. Whether it's watching a massive NFC North showdown on CBS between the Lions and Bears or tuning into one of the best college basketball games of the week between No. 11 Michigan State and Arkansas, Thanksgiving will have something for everybody.

Michigan State star Jeremy Fears Jr. was named Preseason Player of the Year by CBS Sports and has looked the part through the first three weeks of the season. Fears, who is the No. 35 ranked player on CBS Sports Prospect Rankings for the 2027 NBA Draft, is also improving his draft stock ahead of a wide-open draft with his play.

If Fears is drafted in the first round this summer, he will join exclusive company with his brother Jeremiah Fears, who was selected No. 8 overall by the Pelicans in 2025. The Fears brothers could become the latest siblings to both get drafted in the first round of the NBA Draft if Jeremy is selected on the first day.

Here is a list of siblings who were both drafted in the first round of the NBA Draft.

Fears isn't the only notable sibling playing college basketball this season. Bryce James, the son of LeBron James, started the first three games of the season for Arizona. Kiyan Anthony, the son of NBA legend Carmelo Anthony, has been a key rotation piece for Syracuse this season. Andrej Stojaković, the son of one of the greatest shooters in NBA history (Peja Stojaković), has played like an All-American this season.

Here are some of the most notable college basketball players playing this season with NBA bloodlines in their family.

Basketball bloodline: Brother of Jeremiah Fears, who plays for the Pelicans

The Fears brothers will have a chance to become the next set of brothers drafted in the first round of the NBA Draft. Jeremiah had a standout one-and-done season at Oklahoma before becoming a lottery pick. Jeremy redshirted during the 2023-24 season after being shot in the leg. Over the last three seasons, Jeremy has emerged as one of the best players in college basketball. He led the nation in assists last season and is on pace to do the same this season.

Basketball bloodline: Son of Peja Stojaković, former NBA All-Star who played for Kings, Pacers, Hornets and Raptors from 1998-2011

Andrej has a completely different skill set than his father, who lit up the NBA in the 2000s as one of the best 3-point shooters in the sport. Andrej is off to an incredible start to the 2026-27 season, highlighted by a 46-point outburst against Duke, in which 12 of his 14 field-goal makes came from inside the arc. Andrej is playing like an All-American this season and is helping Illinois maintain a top-ranked offense without David Mirković in the lineup.

Basketball bloodlines: Son of LeBron James, NBA's all-time leading scorer who currently plays for 76ers, brother of Bronny James, who plays for the Lakers

The son of one of the most famous athletes on the planet began the season as a starter for Arizona while coach Tommy Lloyd was trying to build his rotation in the midst of the RJ Godfrey eligibility dilemma. James does have bragging rights over his older brother and father because he was part of the Wildcats' Final Four roster last season, something no one in his family had done before.

Basketball bloodline: Son of Gilbert Arenas, a three-time NBA All-Star during an NBA career that spanned from 2001-12 with the Warriors, Wizards, Magic and Grizzlies

After playing in 14 games last season, Arenas returned to USC for his sophomore season. It's looking like the right decision. Gilbert's son has developed into one of the best scorers in college basketball, averaging 21.3 points per game. Arenas has also boosted his draft stock tremendously and could be a lottery pick this summer.

Basketball bloodline: Son of Carmelo Anthony, a Syracuse legend who played for Nuggets, Knicks, Thunder, Rockets, Trail Blazers and Lakers from 2003-2022

After appearing in 29 games last season at his father's alma mater, Anthony decided to return to Syracuse for his sophomore season. Anthony is Syracuse's leading scorer (13.5 points per game) despite coming off the bench in all six games this season.

Basketball bloodlines: Son of Carlos Boozer, who played for the Cavaliers, Jazz, Bulls and Lakers from 2002-15; brother of Cameron Boozer, a rookie for the Grizzlies after playing for the Blue Devils last season

With Cameron Boozer declaring for the NBA Draft, this season marked the first time Cayden didn't play on the same team as his brother. Boozer returned to Duke for his sophomore season instead of entering the transfer portal and has started five of his team's first six games this season and is averaging 6.2 points and 4.3 assists.

Basketball bloodline: Son of Scottie Pippen, a Naismith Hall-of-Famer after his 17-season NBA career with the Bulls, Rockets and Trail Blazers

Pippen is at his third school in three seasons after previous stops at Michigan and Cal. In six games at Ohio State, Pippen is averaging 11.5 points, which ranks third on the team. He finished last season as Cal's second-leading scorer before entering the transfer portal.

Basketball bloodlines: Son of Jason Richardson who played for the Warriors, Bobcats, Suns, Magic and 76ers in 14 seasons in NBA; brother of Jase Richardson, who plays for the Magic

Richardson, who was the No. 28-ranked recruit in the 2026 recruiting cycle by 247Sports, has appeared in four games this season for the Crimson Tide. Richardson started the Crimson Tide's season opener against Sam Houston State, where he finished with four points in 15 minutes.

Basketball bloodline: Son of Andre Iguodala, a four-time NBA champion during his career with the 76ers, Nuggets, Warriors and Heat from 2004-23

Iguodala, who was a three-star recruit in the 2025 recruiting cycle by 247Sports, did not appear in a regular season game during his freshman year. However, the son of the former NBA Finals MVP has appeared in four games this season for the Bears.

Basketball bloodline: Son of Trevor Ariza, an 18-year NBA veteran who won an NBA championship with the 2008-09 Lakers

Ariza, who was a four-star recruit in the 2026 recruiting cycle by 247Sports, is currently playing his freshman season at Oregon. Ariza has made four appearances off the bench and is averaging 5.0 points per game.

Basketball bloodline: Brother of DaRon Holmes II, who currently plays for the Nuggets

Holmes, the No. 36 player in the 2026 recruiting cycle by 247Sports, is looking like a key rotational piece for the Wildcats. The brother of the former first-round pick out of Dayton has made six appearances off the bench this season for the No. 8 Wildcats.

Basketball bloodline: Son of Dominique Wilkins, who is in the Naismith Hall of Fame after playing for the Hawks, Clippers, Celtics, Spurs during his long NBA career

The son of one of the greatest dunkers in NBA history made 32 games off the bench for Georgia last season before transferring to play for the Golden Bears. He has started seven games this season for Cal.

Basketball bloodline: Son of Jermaine O'Neal Sr., who played in NBA from 1996-2014 for the Trail Blazers, Pacers and several other teams

The son of the former six-time NBA All-Star is having a breakout season at SMU. After making 34 appearances last season, O'Neal has started all six of SMU's games this season and is averaging 12.3 points per game.

Basketball bloodline: Son of Hakeem Olajuwon, a Naismith Hall-of-Famer after playing for the Rockets and Raptors from 1984-2002

The former four-star recruit has been a key piece for coach Kyle Smith this season. Olajuwon has appeared in six games (four starts) and is averaging 7 points per game. Notably, his younger brother, Malik Olajuwon, committed to and signed with SMU to play next season.

Basketball bloodline: Son of Brandon Bass, who played in the NBA from 2005-17

Bass has made six appearances off the bench thus far during his freshman season at FSU. His best performance came in Florida State's first game, where he dropped 13 points against Florida A&M.

Basketball bloodline: Son of Mo Williams, who played in NBA for 13 seasons, winning an NBA title with the Cavaliers in 2016

Williams is playing his freshman season at the same place where his father is an assistant coach. The former four-star recruit has been a key rotation piece for Mark Pope this season and is averaging 7.2 points off the bench.

Basketball bloodline: Twin brother of Cooper Flagg, who was the No. 1 pick in the NBA Draft after playing for Duke

The twin brother of the No. 1 pick in the 2025 NBA Draft had to wait an extra year to play college basketball. That's because Cooper reclassified to join Duke in time for the 2024-25 season, while his brother played his senior season in high school. After making 32 appearances last season for Maine, mostly off the bench, Ace has started seven games for the Black Bears and is averaging 6.4 points.

Basketball bloodline: Son of Penny Hardaway, a four-time All-Star during his 14-year NBA career

The son of the current Memphis coach has had quite the college journey. He had two separate stints playing for his father at Memphis before transferring to Coastal Carolina this offseason. He has started one game this season at his new school.

Basketball bloodline: Son of Brandon Roy, the Rookie of the Year in 2006-07 while playing for the Trail Blazers before his NBA career ended after a season with the Timberwolves in 2012-13

The son of the former Portland Trail Blazers star is in his second season at Washington. He has appeared in seven total games during his first two seasons at the college level.

Basketball bloodline: Son of Richard Hamilton, who played for the Wizards, Pistons and Bulls from 1999-2013

The son of the former three-time NBA All-Star is in his freshman season at Oakland. He has six appearances off the bench this season.

#2454. Essay: Escape – MX

von Next Generation am 06.02.2026 in den Kategorien Opinion mit 3 Kommentaren

A few thoughts and reflections on the analysis bubble.

Humans want to understand. A fundamental need of our species eventually developed a concept for the desire to understand and to derive understanding: analysis. Carried through the centuries and applied primarily in literature, this drive increasingly found its way into the comparative physical activity of humans-sport. It fascinates hundreds of thousands of people every weekend; the urge to comprehend the logic – even where there is none – behind the results has become ever more omnipresent. Yet analysis existed long before people fully understood what analysis was – analyzing no longer becomes analysis simply because one is aware of doing it. Tracing the philosophical origins of analysis, pure analysis is merely a subform of communication: communicating by breaking down a whole into parts.

If we understand analysis as part of a larger communication context, it is hardly surprising that analytical formats in Europe developed primarily through blogs and digital platforms – parallel to the ongoing technologization of the world. Analysis has always existed, but only with the internet did it gain new relevance: communication could, for the first time, reach a potentially unlimited audience permanently. This explains an apparent contradiction of its origins: analysis exists continuously, yet it is always dependent on its recipients. Without an audience, it has no effect. In the words of Niklas Luhmann, communication does not arise from mere sending, but from understanding on the part of the receiver. Analysis is therefore not an isolated act, but an interactive process.

In the age of social media, however, this dependence increasingly leads to a dead end. Highly complex matters are expected to be made understandable, consumable, and entertaining within thirty seconds. Paradoxically, social media produces more recipients than ever – and simultaneously a structural scarcity of attention. Georg Franck refers to this as the “attention economy,” in which visibility, rather than truth or depth, becomes the central currency. For a long time, analysis was a dialogical process: presenting, structuring, weighing – a reciprocal interplay between sender and receiver, reliant on resonance and reflection. Jürgen Habermas’ concept of communicative action captures exactly this: understanding emerges where arguments are given time and space. In short-form formats, communication continues- often with enormous reach- but the channels through which it occurs have shifted.

“A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.” – Herbert A. Simon

Analysis increasingly degenerates into a tool for tabloid-style exaggeration. Headlines such as “THE NEW TACTIC,” “THE BEST PRESSING IN THE WORLD,” or “THIS IS MODERN FOOTBALL” suggest analysis but primarily follow market logic. Analyses are linguistically amplified as if they must be sold: the newest product, the best of its kind, faster, higher, further. Football as a consumer product is established – but now even the idyllic backyard of analysis? Marshall McLuhan’s famous dictum, “The medium is the message,” becomes particularly tangible here: the format determines not only the form, but increasingly also the content of analysis itself. The task is to reclaim analysis as a pursuit of understanding and curb its reduction to a consumable, attention-driven product – perhaps the challenge of the modern era is not to reinvent analysis, but to restore time, depth, and dialogical capacity to it.

To continue the metaphor of the idyllic backyard: analysis is increasingly turning into a bustling city. Here a street vendor, there a shop – no, I don’t want to buy anything. Help, where have I ended up? Everything crowded, everyone stressed, everyone caught in the rush of striving, of wanting. I just want the idyll: a coffee, some calm, a deep conversation. But the idyll is dead. Perhaps, as an analyst, one sometimes feels a certain emptiness – a metropolitan melancholy – the emptiness of overstimulated impersonality.

“The metropolitan is compelled by the economy of money exchange to a precision and objectivity that deprives personal life of its warmth.” – Georg Simmel, The Metropolises and the Intellectual Life, 1903

But let us zoom out again: I often experience this feeling on “X” or YouTube. There is an abundance of information, often highlighted for attention. Yet more information on complex topics does not automatically lead to more knowledge; it generates noise – a noise I described earlier in the metaphor. This constant noise simultaneously depletes the already scarce resource of attention and creates a perpetual stimulus environment, leading to a lack of contextualization and interpretation, while leaving many exhausted-another tactic video, another tweet, another reel on the best pressing? Phew – this “phew” is what science calls fragmented cognition. Algorithms naturally amplify extremes-even in sports: outrage, “ALL-CAPS HEADLINES,” or promotion drive engagement.

This critique is not aimed at users or analysts; we are all trapped in a system with incentive structures. Nevertheless, I want to draw attention to the growing bubbleization and ideological polarization of the analysis scene, amplified by extremes and a lack of contextualization. Quick accessibility and democratization lead to information, to knowledge, but this abundance also produces a depletion of theory and balance. We experience a pseudo – plurality in sport, an implied logic in the game that does not exist, manifested by algorithms – through likes and views.

A concrete example: relationism. A fascinating topic, scarcely explored-yet the mere word triggers algorithmic attention so heavily that it is used excessively, reducing it to a black-and-white concept and establishing a dogma, rather than allowing proper theoretical discussion. How do we get out of this situation? Everyone has taste, everyone has preferences – yes, everyone has their dogmas. We are human – accept it. As René Marić once said, dogmas can be dissolved by connecting them, by allowing different ideas to meet. Or as Jamie Hamilton puts it: perceive analysis as aesthetics. If we understand football as aesthetics, then football becomes art – but what is art? Art is the undefinable. And if we accept football as something without logic, we may at least free ourselves from established regimens of thinking and dogma. Don’t let yourselves be confined – feel the aesthetics.

“We live in a world where there is more and more information, and less and less meaning.” – Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation, 1981

If we turn to history, literary philosophy shows us that even the concept of freedom divides opinion – does freedom enable analysis, or does it simply reinforce the status quo and thereby prevent true analysis? Perhaps, however, this is not the real question. Maybe it is not about freedom versus non-freedom, but about whether we understand logic as the opposite of freedom. Logicimplies binary outcomes – true or false, right or wrong – and this stands in tension with the ‘spirit of play’. Play has rules and objectives, yet within the act of playing there are no universal truths. The growing sense of uniformity and rehearsal – the impression that everyone plays in similar ways – often creates the feeling that the game follows the rules of a single, universal logic, as if logic determines play rather than play shaping logic.

My concern is less about what is objectively right or wrong in football, and more about how we, as analysts and coaches, sometimes present our ideas as universal truths. By doing so, we implicitly suggest that there exists a pure logic within the game – a logic that may not fundamentally exist. I would argue that sport exists primarily to evoke emotions in those who play and those who watch – an experience that can be understood through aesthetics, where art becomes a counterpoint to logic, as Tolstoy suggested. This challenges the belief that results or success should stand above everything else and dictate our styles of play.

If there is no single ‘true’ way to play, then there can also be no single true analysis that fully dissects it into definitive parts. That is why we must give space to the diffuse edges – even at the risk of weakening clarity or precision in our explanations – and accept that not everything can be clearly identified or categorized, because pure logic does not exist here. Yet I firmly believe that by allowing more room for uncertainty and ambiguity within the game, we open ourselves to entirely new worlds of understanding. And precisely for this reason, it is all the more important to ask ourselves who we are-and what we want to be as analysts. We must no longer divide ourselves into “us” and “them,” but understand ourselves as a shared form of football observer. Hannah Arendt describes thinking as an activity that only unfolds in exchange, as something that emerges in the “in-between” of people. Analysis, therefore, is not a possession, but a process. We need to dare more again: recognize our own (natural!) weaknesses in reasoning, disclose our personal assumptions, and discuss more honestly with one another. Know more of what we do not know and never will.

For this reason, I am skeptical of sharply distinguishing between universally trained and didactically trained analysts – or of job advertisements favoring only one type. Pierre Bourdieu shows that fields tend to stabilize through differentiation rather than understanding; separation becomes a social marker rather than a question of quality. Class war! Is that really what we want? Pitting the professionalization of sport against an open culture? This runs all the way from coach education to analyst circles: those who were never professionals are excluded. Those who do not meet the standards in general education also do not meet the standards in football. It is a coupling of market logic with football – and we need a return to open football, even if this openness, in some places, requires a degree of self-criticism that is uncomfortable for some decision maker. Breaking out of established logics also means accepting that logic cannot be predetermined.

“Technology is never neutral; it always changes the conditions under which knowledge is recognized.” – Neil Postman, Technopoly, 1992

Attempts to standardize analysis this way lead to the imposition of linear thinking – a workflowization of analysis. The constant noise of information overload reinforces this effect. Increasingly, I observe a communicatively insulated bubble of club-based analysts, where external exchange is hardly desired. Yet the core of analysis is forgotten: “Thinking without communication is empty,” writes Jürgen Habermas-knowledge emerges in dialogue. Analysis thrives on joint dissection, on contradiction, and on critical (self-) questioning.

This text is not a judgment of the scene. Rather, it is an expression of unease-a self-reflective judgment. I, too, have long allowed myself to be guided by factions, by the pursuit of jobs, by the pursuit of attention, and I became dependent on it. Only when I became aware of this and adopted a more didactic path – without a goal beyond curiosity about the game – did new worlds of football open up to me. A curiosity expressed not in truths, but in provisional knowledge; in perspectives rather than dogmas; in theory as a tool rather than a label. Perhaps our strength should not lie in being faster, louder, or bigger. Perhaps it lies in withstanding the noise of the digital age. Where analysis no longer allows contradiction, it ends. But it also ends where analysis becomes mere consumption. But to end the text on a positive note – at the same time, there are more opportunities than ever before, more tactical cameras than ever, and more games to analyze than ever.

There have been discussions surrounding the importance of aesthetics as a branch of philosophy. Beauty is subjective and it has led to categorizations of protagonist and antagonist in the case of ball possession despite no concrete proof that control of the game belongs to teams with high possession. This has created villains and heroes; some have been/become victims of this categorization. Maybe in the place of aesthetics we can propose statistics. Considering that the scoreline is a statistic (with all the negative connotations around it e.g “lies, damned lies and statistics”- Mark Twain., it really has not stood a chance), analysis should be data/statistically driven as findings, conclusions and discussions will be more objective.

#2451. Jerry Jones refutes Aaron Rodgers' accusations, calls Mike McCarthy 'outstanding'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ARLINGTON, Texas -- Aaron Rodgers nuked Pittsburgh Steelers coach Mike McCarthy's reputation after the Steelers benched him late Tuesday night.

In a scathing appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show" on ESPN on Wednesday, the four-time NFL MVP and Super Bowl XLV MVP ripped McCarthy, saying Steelers tight end Pat Freiermuth told him of Pittsburgh's decision to make him inactive for Friday's game against the Denver Broncos, and he accused McCarthy of sleeping and being late to team meetings throughout the season. Rodgers raised numerous other accusations against McCarthy, including that he arrived late this week and slept during offensive meetings.

Rodgers said that the behavior McCarthy exhibited this season in Pittsburgh was present during their shared tenure with the Green Bay Packers, as well as during McCarthy's run as head coach of the Dallas Cowboys. The Cowboys employed McCarthy as their head coach for five seasons from 2020 to 2024, and they went 49-35 in that span, tied for the eighth-best record in the league with the Minnesota Vikings. Dallas won 12 games in the regular season for three consecutive years from 2021 to 2023, the first time the franchise accomplished that feat since their 1990s Super Bowl dynasty teams. The Cowboys went 1-3 in the postseason under McCarthy, advancing no further than the NFC divisional round.

"They know what's going on. Like I said, they all know. Everybody knows," Rodgers said on Wednesday. "Just like the guys in Green Bay knew. It's like the people in Dallas knew. Like they know what the deal is."

One of the people in Dallas who claimed not to know what Rodgers was talking about is Cowboys owner and general manager Jerry Jones. Jones unequivocally refuted Rodgers' claims and said he tried to extend McCarthy when his original five-year contract expired at the end of the 2024 season. The two sides couldn't come to an agreement on a new deal, so McCarthy took a year off in 2025 before being hired by the Steelers this year.

"I never saw anything that would not ... I offered him to stay at least another year when he left. I thought he was outstanding as the head coach, and [he] had a great command of quarterback, offense. Can't say enough good things about him. He's frankly one of the finest people around football that I have been around. I can't say enough about him. I never had the type of thing that's being said about him, I've never had that in consideration at any of my time with him. [Whether it was] extending his contract or any of that. That [alleged behavior] was never on the table."

While Rodgers painted a picture of extremely erratic and irresponsible behavior by his longtime head coach, Jones claims none of that happened in Dallas.
